title: Brazil's cultural life is digitally domestic, while cultural policy has high approval despite low public awareness
source_unit: Brazil Ministry of Culture, Hábitos e Consumo de Cultura / Percepções sobre as Políticas Culturais
geography: Brazil; all 27 federative units; adults aged 16 and above

observations.period: November 6-12, 2025; cultural consumption in the last 30 days

denominator.unit: Nexus household interviews with adults aged 16 and above across Brazil's 27 federative units

music_consumption.unit: percent reporting music consumption in the last 30 days

film_consumption.unit: percent reporting film consumption in the last 30 days

series_consumption.unit: percent reporting series consumption in the last 30 days

soap_opera_consumption.unit: percent reporting soap-opera consumption in the last 30 days

sports_spectacle_consumption.unit: percent reporting sports-spectacle consumption in the last 30 days

physical_book_consumption.unit: percent reporting physical-book consumption in the last 30 days

digital_game_consumption.unit: percent reporting digital-game consumption in the last 30 days

ebook_audiobook_consumption.unit: percent reporting ebook or audiobook consumption in the last 30 days

theater_consumption.unit: percent reporting theater consumption in the last 30 days

mechanism.value: Easy-access, screen- and audio-mediated cultural consumption dominates the reported cultural basket, with books and venue-based forms reaching smaller shares

observations.method: Nexus quantitative survey commissioned by Brazil's Ministry of Culture; household interviews, adults aged 16+, quota controls for sex, age, labor-force participation, region, and municipality type, followed by weighting.
observations.uncertainty: The measures are self-reported reach indicators, not expenditure, minutes, frequency-adjusted engagement, or verified transactions; categories may overlap.
observations.subgroup: Adults aged 16 and above across all 27 Brazilian federative units.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower reported venue or book reach may reflect recall, access, wording, or the 30-day window rather than a durable preference against in-person culture.

observations.period: November 6-12, 2025; reported barriers, media access, and intended cultural return

denominator.unit: Nexus household interviews with adults aged 16 and above across Brazil's 27 federative units

lack_of_time_barrier.unit: percent naming lack of time as a barrier to cultural participation

lack_of_interest_barrier.unit: percent naming lack of interest as a barrier to cultural participation

lack_of_money_barrier.unit: percent naming lack of money as a barrier to cultural participation

mobile_phone_primary_medium.unit: percent identifying the cell phone as a principal medium for cultural consumption

television_medium.unit: percent identifying television as a medium for cultural consumption

want_more_cinema.unit: percent intending to attend more cinema

want_more_music_shows.unit: percent intending to attend more music shows or festivals

want_more_theater.unit: percent intending to attend more theater

mechanism.value: Time and distribution constraints are more prominent than money alone, while demand for shared, in-person cultural experiences remains visible

observations.method: The report combines structured survey questions on barriers, media, and intended participation with qualitative focus groups conducted across capitals/metropolitan areas and interior locations.
observations.uncertainty: Barrier responses are perceptions and do not identify causal constraints; intended attendance is not realized attendance, and medium-use shares do not establish exclusivity.
observations.subgroup: Adults aged 16 and above; quantitative estimates are national survey results and qualitative findings are not population estimates.
observations.counterinterpretation: The prominence of time may partly capture competing work, care, or commuting demands, while the desire for cinema and shows could reflect episodic rather than sustained demand.

observations.period: November 6-12, 2025; awareness and perceived legitimacy of cultural policy

denominator.unit: Nexus household interviews with adults aged 16 and above across Brazil's 27 federative units

policy_awareness_known.unit: percent who knew of the Paulo Gustavo and Aldir Blanc cultural laws

policy_awareness_heard_not_understood.unit: percent who had heard of the laws but did not know how they worked

policy_no_awareness.unit: percent reporting no awareness of the Paulo Gustavo and Aldir Blanc cultural laws

decentralized_law_approval.unit: percent approving the Paulo Gustavo and Aldir Blanc laws

policies_improve_federal_government_imag.unit: percent saying cultural policies improve the federal government's image

policies_improve_president_image.unit: percent saying cultural policies improve the President's image

government_more_on_side_of_people.unit: percent saying cultural policy makes government seem more on the side of Brazilian people

government_more_distant.unit: percent saying cultural policy makes government seem more distant

municipal_government_perceived_culture_a.unit: percent naming city governments as the government level doing most for culture

federal_government_perceived_culture_act.unit: percent naming the federal government as the government level doing most for culture

mechanism.value: Cultural policy can carry symbolic legitimacy and approval beyond detailed policy comprehension, but the gap between approval and awareness limits claims about informed mandate

observations.method: National survey questions on awareness, approval, perceived government image, and perceived distance or proximity; the report also includes four qualitative focus groups.
observations.uncertainty: These are commissioned perception measures, not causal estimates of policy effects or independent measures of government legitimacy; question wording and political context matter.
observations.subgroup: Adults aged 16 and above across all 27 federative units; focus groups included adults aged 18-50 from capitals/metropolitan areas and interior locations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Approval may reflect broad support for culture or social benefits rather than knowledge of the named laws, and image effects may not translate into durable institutional trust or electoral behavior.

related_sources.claim: Brazil Ministry of Culture landing page announcing the survey and its findings.
Official 68-page report with quantitative fieldwork, focus-group method, cultural consumption, barriers, and policy-perception results.

boundary: This record adds Brazilian evidence on cultural reach, access constraints, intended venue return, and perceived legitimacy of cultural policy. It is a commissioned self-report survey with qualitative context, not transaction data, causal policy evaluation, or a direct measure of durable institutional trust.
